questions.question: What is an embedded server in Spring Boot and why is it useful?
questions.title: Spring Boot embedded server explained
questions.direct_answer: An embedded server is a web server that the Spring Boot application carries as a dependency and manages as part of its own lifecycle. A servlet application normally gets Tomcat from `spring-boot-starter-web`, so starting the application also starts the HTTP server. This makes the application easy to run, test, and deploy as one versioned unit.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The server is an application dependency, not a separately installed application server.
The server and the Spring `ApplicationContext` normally run in the same JVM process.
`spring-boot-starter-web` uses embedded Tomcat by default in Spring Boot 3.3.1.
The application can be packaged as an executable JAR and started with `java -jar`.
Keeping the server version with the application makes environments easier to reproduce.
Embedded deployment is a deployment choice; it does not automatically make the application a microservice.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An embedded server in Spring Boot is a web server that is added to the application as a dependency and managed by the application itself. In a normal Spring MVC project, `spring-boot-starter-web` brings embedded Tomcat. When `SpringApplication.run` creates the web `ApplicationContext`, Boot configures and starts Tomcat in the same JVM.

For example, an order service can be built as `orders.jar` and started with `java -jar orders.jar`. That single command starts the Spring beans, controller mappings, and HTTP server. The team does not first install a separate Tomcat instance and copy a WAR into it.

This model is useful because the server version travels with the application. A developer laptop, a test job, and a production container can run the same application-server combination. It also gives the application one clear lifecycle: if startup fails, the server is not left running separately, and closing the `ApplicationContext` stops the server.

The word embedded describes ownership and lifecycle, not only a physical JAR layout. During IDE development, the server libraries may simply be on the classpath; the server is still embedded because the application creates and owns it. Spring Boot can also build a WAR for an external servlet container when an organization needs traditional deployment.

So the main benefit is a repeatable, self-contained way to run a web application. Ports, TLS, thread limits, timeouts, monitoring, and graceful shutdown still need proper production configuration.

sections.title: Embedded server ownership and startup
sections.content:
**Traditional and embedded deployment**

In traditional servlet deployment, an operations team installs a server such as Tomcat. The application is packaged as a WAR and deployed into that running server. The server owns the listening port and can host more than one application.

With an embedded server, the direction is reversed. The application includes a server implementation as a dependency. Spring Boot creates a web-aware `ApplicationContext`, finds a `ServletWebServerFactory`, builds the server, connects Spring MVC to it, and starts it during context refresh. The application process therefore owns both the Spring container and the HTTP server.

**What the starter actually does**

`spring-boot-starter-web` selects the common Spring MVC libraries and the Tomcat starter. It does not contain the business endpoint. The application's controller supplies `/status`; Boot supplies the normal MVC and server infrastructure needed to receive the request and dispatch it to that controller.

When the application is built with the Spring Boot plugin, its classes and runtime dependencies can be packaged into an executable JAR. `java -jar` uses Boot's launcher to create the application classpath and call the main class. The same ownership model also exists when the app runs from an IDE or Maven because the server dependencies are still controlled by the application.

**Why teams use it**

The deployable unit records the application libraries and server version together. That reduces the chance that a working build reaches a machine with a different shared-server library. Local startup is also simple, and a container image can run the application without installing a separate Tomcat distribution.

This convenience is not a promise that every default is right for production. The chosen server still has connection limits, worker resources, TLS settings, logs, and shutdown behaviour. Those settings should come from the needs and measurements of the application.

sections.title: From web dependency to a running endpoint
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  D["spring-boot-starter-web"] --> F["Tomcat server factory is auto-configured"]
  M["SpringApplication.run"] --> C["Web ApplicationContext refreshes"]
  F --> C
  C --> S["Application-owned Tomcat starts"]
  S --> R["HTTP request reaches Spring MVC controller"]
  C -. "context closes" .-> X["Tomcat stops with the application"]
```

questions.question: What is context path in Spring Boot and how do you configure it?
questions.title: Spring Boot context path configuration
questions.direct_answer: In a servlet-based Spring Boot application, the context path is the prefix added before all application routes. It is empty by default. Configure it with `server.servlet.context-path`, for example `/api`; a controller route `/orders` is then served at `/api/orders`. WebFlux uses `spring.webflux.base-path` instead.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The servlet context path mounts the whole application below one URL prefix.
Its default value is empty, which means the application is mounted at `/`.
Set it with `server.servlet.context-path=/api`.
The context path is added before controller mappings; it does not replace them.
WebFlux uses `spring.webflux.base-path`, not the servlet property.
Actuator on the same server is also below the servlet context path.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
In a servlet-based Spring Boot application, the context path is the URL prefix under which the whole web application is mounted. It is empty by default, so a controller mapped to `/orders` is normally reached at `/orders`. Setting `server.servlet.context-path=/api` changes the application URL to `/api/orders`.

The context path does not replace the controller mapping. The server first selects the application using `/api`, and Spring MVC then selects the controller using `/orders`. This is why the final path is the combination `/api/orders`.

For example, with port `8080`, context path `/shop`, and `@GetMapping("/products/{id}")`, product 42 is available at `http://localhost:8080/shop/products/42`. The controller annotation remains `/products/{id}`; only configuration supplies `/shop`.

The property is for servlet applications. A WebFlux application uses `spring.webflux.base-path`. Actuator endpoints on the same server are also below the servlet context path, so the usual health endpoint becomes `/api/actuator/health`. A separate management port has its own management server base-path settings.

A context path is useful when the application must genuinely be mounted below a fixed prefix. If an API gateway only exposes an external prefix and removes it before forwarding, the application can stay at the root. The important point is to know which layer owns each part of the public URL.

sections.title: Build the final URL one layer at a time
sections.content:
**What the context path controls**

A servlet container can mount a web application at the root or below a prefix. Spring Boot exposes that prefix as `server.servlet.context-path`. The default is an empty value, so the application starts at the root path.

Suppose `OrderController` has `@RequestMapping("/orders")`. With no context path, `GET /orders/42` can reach its `/{id}` method. After setting the context path to `/api`, the same controller is reached at `GET /api/orders/42`. The Java mapping does not need `/api` because the server handles that part before Spring MVC chooses a handler.

**Do not mix three different prefixes**

The servlet context path mounts the application. A controller's `@RequestMapping` and `@GetMapping` values identify handlers inside it. `spring.mvc.servlet.path`, when used, maps Spring MVC's `DispatcherServlet` inside the context. These values can combine, but adding several prefixes without a clear need makes URLs harder to reason about.

A reverse proxy or gateway adds another possible layer. It may preserve an external prefix when forwarding, or remove that prefix. The application context path should match the path actually received by the application, not simply copy whatever the browser sees.

**Actuator and reactive applications**

When Actuator shares the main server, its web base path is relative to the servlet context path. With `/api` and the normal Actuator base path, health is available at `/api/actuator/health`. If management uses a separate port, its server and base-path settings determine the management URL.

A reactive WebFlux application has no servlet context. Its corresponding application prefix is `spring.webflux.base-path`. Choosing the property that matches the web stack prevents a configuration value that appears valid but has no effect.

sections.title: Which setting owns each part of the URL?
sections.content:
| Setting | Purpose | Example result |
|---|---|---|
| `server.servlet.context-path=/api` | Mounts the whole servlet application | `/api/orders/42` |
| `@RequestMapping("/orders")` | Groups routes inside the application | `/orders/42` before the context prefix |
| `@GetMapping("/{id}")` | Selects one controller operation | Adds `/42` for the requested id |
| `spring.webflux.base-path=/api` | Sets the application prefix for WebFlux | Reactive route becomes `/api/...` |

questions.question: What embedded servers does Spring Boot support and how do you switch between them?
questions.title: Tomcat vs Jetty vs Undertow in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot 3.3.1 supports Tomcat, Jetty, and Undertow as embedded servlet servers. `spring-boot-starter-web` selects Tomcat by default. To switch, exclude `spring-boot-starter-tomcat` and add the starter for Jetty or Undertow. WebFlux uses Reactor Netty by default and can also run on a supported servlet server.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Spring MVC supports embedded Tomcat, Jetty, and Undertow.
`spring-boot-starter-web` uses Tomcat by default.
Switch servers by replacing dependencies, not by setting a server-name property.
Keep controller code on Spring APIs so it remains portable.
Replace `server.tomcat.*` tuning and Tomcat customizers when moving to another server.
WebFlux defaults to Reactor Netty; server choice and web stack are related but separate decisions.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
For a Spring MVC application, Spring Boot 3.3.1 supports embedded Tomcat, Jetty, and Undertow. `spring-boot-starter-web` brings Tomcat by default. For a WebFlux application, the default server is Reactor Netty, although supported servlet servers can also run the reactive stack.

The switch is made in the build, not with a property. For Maven, I exclude `spring-boot-starter-tomcat` from the web starter and add `spring-boot-starter-jetty` or `spring-boot-starter-undertow`. Boot's dependency management supplies a compatible version.

A normal Spring MVC controller usually does not change because it talks to Spring's web abstractions. Common `server.*` settings, such as the port, also remain available. Server-specific settings and customizers do change; a `server.tomcat.*` property obviously has no meaning after moving to Jetty.

I choose a server from real requirements and measurements: protocol features, organization support, observability, deployment policy, and behaviour under the application's workload. I would not claim that Jetty or Undertow is always faster or uses less memory, because the result depends on versions, configuration, and traffic.

There are also feature boundaries. Spring Boot does not support JSPs in an executable JAR; Tomcat and Jetty can use JSPs with WAR packaging, while Undertow does not support JSPs. After switching, I inspect the dependency tree and run the same HTTP and load tests to confirm that only the intended server is active.

sections.title: Server selection through dependencies
sections.content:
**Servlet and reactive web stacks**

A Spring MVC application uses the Servlet API. In Spring Boot 3.3.1, the supported embedded servlet choices are Tomcat, Jetty, and Undertow. The normal web starter depends on the Tomcat starter, which is why a new MVC application starts Tomcat without naming it in the main class.

Spring WebFlux is the reactive web stack. Its starter brings Reactor Netty by default. WebFlux can also run on Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow, but changing the HTTP server does not turn MVC code into reactive code or the other way around.

**The build selects the implementation**

Spring Boot auto-configuration looks for a supported server implementation on the classpath. A clean switch therefore removes the default Tomcat starter and adds exactly one replacement starter. Boot's dependency management keeps that server aligned with the selected Boot release.

Most controllers continue to work because `@RestController`, mappings, validation, and response types belong to Spring. Configuration that names an implementation is not portable. For example, `server.tomcat.threads.max` and a `TomcatServletWebServerFactory` customizer must be replaced with the corresponding approach for the new server.

**Server-selection criteria and verification**

There is no useful universal ranking in which one server is always fastest. Compare the versions supported by the Boot release, required protocols and view technologies, team experience, logging and metrics needs, and measured results with realistic traffic.

JSP support is a concrete example of a boundary. JSPs are not supported from an executable JAR. With WAR packaging, Tomcat and Jetty can support them, while Undertow does not. A dependency-tree check followed by startup, integration, and load tests is safer than relying on a generic performance label.

sections.title: Server choices in Spring Boot 3.3.1
sections.content:
| Choice | Typical stack | What to remember |
|---|---|---|
| Tomcat | Default for Spring MVC | Mature Servlet server; brought by `spring-boot-starter-web` |
| Jetty | Spring MVC or WebFlux | Add the Jetty starter after excluding the default server |
| Undertow | Spring MVC or WebFlux | Supported alternative; does not support JSP |
| Reactor Netty | Default for WebFlux | Reactive default, not a servlet container |

sections.title: Replace Tomcat with Jetty in a Maven build
sections.content:
```xml
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        <exclusions>
            <exclusion>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
            </exclusion>
        </exclusions>
    </dependency>

    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

Do not add a version to the Jetty starter when the project uses Spring Boot dependency management. Run `mvn dependency:tree` after the change and confirm that Jetty is present and the Tomcat starter is not.

questions.question: How do you configure the embedded Tomcat in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Configuring embedded Tomcat — port, threads, timeout
questions.direct_answer: Configure embedded Tomcat mainly with external properties: common settings such as `server.port`, and Tomcat-specific settings such as `server.tomcat.threads.max`, `server.tomcat.max-connections`, `server.tomcat.accept-count`, and connection timeouts. Use a Tomcat `WebServerFactoryCustomizer` only for settings that properties do not expose, and choose capacity values from measurements rather than fixed interview numbers.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use `server.port` for the HTTP port and `server.tomcat.*` for Tomcat-specific options.
`threads.max` limits servlet worker threads.
`max-connections` limits connections accepted and processed at one time.
`accept-count` limits the pending connection queue when capacity is busy.
`connection-timeout` waits for the request URI line; it is not a controller deadline.
Use `WebServerFactoryCustomizer` only when a suitable property is unavailable.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Embedded Tomcat is normally configured through Spring Boot properties. Common server settings use `server.*`, while Tomcat-specific settings use `server.tomcat.*`. For example, `server.port` changes the listening port and `server.tomcat.threads.max` limits the Tomcat worker pool. I use a `WebServerFactoryCustomizer` only when the required Tomcat option is not exposed as a property.

The capacity settings describe different stages. `max-connections` limits connections that Tomcat accepts and processes at one time. `accept-count` limits the pending operating-system queue when the server cannot immediately take another connection. `threads.max` limits worker threads that execute servlet requests. Raising one value does not automatically remove a limit at another stage.

`server.tomcat.connection-timeout` is not a controller execution timeout. It is the time Tomcat waits after accepting a connection for the request URI line. `keep-alive-timeout` controls how long an idle keep-alive connection waits for another request. Database, HTTP-client, and end-to-end request deadlines need separate configuration.

For an API on port `8081`, I might start with an explicit worker limit, connection cap, pending queue, and duration values in `application.properties`. Those numbers are examples, not universal recommendations. I would load-test the real endpoint and watch request latency, active threads, connection counts, queueing, CPU, memory, and downstream pools.

The useful interview point is that Tomcat tuning is a capacity decision, not a list of magic numbers. A very large worker pool can increase memory and downstream contention, while a large queue can hide overload by increasing latency. I set a bounded starting point, measure, and make sure the database and other downstream services can handle the same concurrency.

sections.title: Tomcat connection and worker capacity
sections.content:
**Property-based Tomcat configuration**

Spring Boot binds common web-server settings from `server.*` and Tomcat-only settings from `server.tomcat.*`. External properties keep the same application build usable in development, test, and production. The environment can change the port or limits without recompiling Java code.

A connection first reaches Tomcat's connector. `server.tomcat.max-connections` caps the connections Tomcat accepts and processes at one time. When the server cannot take more immediately, the operating system may hold pending connection attempts up to the `accept-count` limit. A connection beyond the available capacity can wait, time out, or be refused depending on the network and operating system.

**A connection is not the same as a worker thread**

HTTP keep-alive allows one accepted connection to carry more than one request over time. A Tomcat worker handles a servlet request while application code is running. `server.tomcat.threads.max` bounds that worker pool, and `threads.min-spare` keeps a minimum number available. Connection, worker, and downstream-pool limits therefore describe different resources.

**Connection and keep-alive timeout semantics**

`server.tomcat.connection-timeout` measures how long the connector waits after accepting a connection for the request URI line. It does not stop a controller that has already been running for too long. `server.tomcat.keep-alive-timeout` waits for the next request on an existing connection. An application that calls a database or another API needs suitable timeouts in those clients as well.

**Tune with evidence**

A high thread count is not automatically faster. More simultaneous requests can consume more memory, increase context switching, and exhaust a smaller database pool. A large pending queue can turn overload into long latency. Start from an explicit, reviewable configuration, exercise realistic endpoints, and observe the entire request path before changing one limit.

sections.title: Where each Tomcat setting applies
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C["Client opens a connection"] --> N{"Below max-connections?"}
  N -- "yes" --> A["Tomcat accepts connection"]
  N -- "no" --> Q["Pending OS queue up to accept-count"]
  Q -. "capacity opens" .-> A
  Q --> R["Excess attempt waits, times out, or is refused"]
  A --> U["Request URI line before connection-timeout"]
  U --> W["Worker available within threads.max"]
  W --> M["Spring MVC controller"]
```

sections.title: An explicit, measurable starting configuration
sections.content:
```properties
# Illustrative values; validate them with the real workload.
server.port=8081
server.tomcat.threads.max=160
server.tomcat.threads.min-spare=20
server.tomcat.max-connections=4096
server.tomcat.accept-count=100
server.tomcat.connection-timeout=5s
server.tomcat.keep-alive-timeout=20s
```

These properties configure the connector and worker resources. They do not set a five-second controller timeout. If an order endpoint calls a database and a payment API, those clients need their own connection and response timeouts, and their pools must be sized with the server concurrency in mind.

questions.question: How do you configure HTTPS for the Spring Boot embedded server?
questions.title: HTTPS configuration in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Give the embedded server a certificate and private key, then bind that material to its connector. In Spring Boot 3.3.1, define a named JKS/PKCS12 or PEM SSL bundle and reference it with `server.ssl.bundle`; set the HTTPS port with `server.port`. Keep passwords and keys outside source control. A reverse proxy may terminate TLS instead of the application.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: HTTPS requires a certificate chain and its matching private key.
An SSL bundle gives the key material a reusable name.
Set `server.ssl.bundle=<name>` and choose the connector port with `server.port`.
A PKCS12 or JKS keystore can hold the server key; PEM certificate and key files are also supported.
A server truststore is needed for client-certificate verification, not normal one-way HTTPS.
TLS can instead terminate at a trusted reverse proxy or load balancer.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
To serve HTTPS directly, the embedded server needs a certificate chain and the matching private key. In Spring Boot 3.3.1, a clear approach is to define those materials as a named SSL bundle and point `server.ssl.bundle` to that bundle. A PKCS12 file can hold the server certificate, chain, and private key.

For example, I can create a JKS-style bundle named `web` whose keystore is `file:/run/secrets/server.p12`, supply its password through an environment variable, set `server.ssl.bundle=web`, and listen on port `8443`. The embedded connector then performs the TLS handshake before an HTTP request reaches Spring MVC.

The server keystore proves the server's identity. The calling browser or service must trust the certificate issuer on its side. A server truststore is not required for ordinary one-way HTTPS; it is needed when the server must verify client certificates for mutual TLS.

Many production systems terminate TLS at a trusted load balancer or ingress and send HTTP to the application over a protected internal network. In that design, the proxy owns the public certificate. The application must trust forwarded headers only from known proxies so redirects and generated links use the original HTTPS scheme correctly.

The normal Boot properties configure one main connector as HTTP or HTTPS. Serving both directly requires server-specific programmatic connector configuration; often a proxy and an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect are simpler. I keep private keys and passwords outside source control, verify the full certificate chain and hostname, and test renewal before expiry.

In Spring Boot 3.3.1, a clear approach is to define those materials as a named SSL bundle and point `server.ssl.bundle` to that bundle. A PKCS12 file can hold the server certificate, chain, and private key.

beats.spokenText: The server keystore proves the server's identity. The calling browser or service must trust the certificate issuer on its side. A server truststore is not required for ordinary one-way HTTPS; it is needed when the server must verify client certificates for mutual TLS.

beats.cue: Compare direct TLS with proxy termination
beats.spokenText: Many production systems terminate TLS at a trusted load balancer or ingress and send HTTP to the application over a protected internal network. In that design, the proxy owns the public certificate. The application must trust forwarded headers only from known proxies so redirects and generated links use the original HTTPS scheme correctly.

The normal Boot properties configure one main connector as HTTP or HTTPS. Serving both directly requires server-specific programmatic connector configuration; often a proxy and an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect are simpler. I keep private keys and passwords outside source control, verify the full certificate chain and hostname, and test renewal before expiry.
beats.recallRule: Keystore gives the server an identity; truststore verifies the peer when peer authentication is required.

sections.title: Certificate material and TLS termination
sections.content:
**What the server must prove**

Before HTTP data is exchanged over HTTPS, the server presents a certificate chain and proves that it holds the corresponding private key. The client checks the hostname, validity period, chain, and trusted issuer. Only after that TLS handshake succeeds does Tomcat pass the decrypted HTTP request to Spring MVC.

Spring Boot can read key material from direct `server.ssl.*` properties or from a named SSL bundle. A bundle keeps the location, store type, password, key alias, protocol options, and related material together. The embedded server refers to that name through `server.ssl.bundle`.

**Keystore and truststore have different jobs**

For ordinary HTTPS, the server's keystore contains its private key and certificate chain. The client has its own trust anchors and decides whether to trust that chain. A truststore configured on the server becomes important for mutual TLS, where the server also asks the client for a certificate and verifies it.

PKCS12 is a common portable file format for the key and certificates. PEM files can hold the certificate and private key separately. The file format does not remove the need to protect the private key and password. Mount them from a secret store or secured file path rather than committing them to the repository.

**Application and proxy TLS termination**

The application can terminate TLS itself, or a load balancer, gateway, or ingress can terminate it first. Direct termination keeps the TLS endpoint in the application. Proxy termination centralizes certificate operations, but the connection from proxy to application must follow the organization's network-security policy.

When a proxy terminates TLS, the application may receive plain HTTP even though the user called HTTPS. Forwarded-header handling must be configured for the deployment, and only trusted proxies should be allowed to supply those headers. This prevents a caller from forging scheme or host information.

**Test the real contract**

A successful application startup is not enough. Test the public hostname, certificate chain, supported protocol, redirect behaviour, and expiry monitoring from outside the service. If client certificates are required, also test a valid client, a missing certificate, and an untrusted certificate.

sections.title: Choose the TLS termination point
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  C["HTTPS client"] --> D{"Where does TLS end?"}
  D -- "embedded server" --> S["Tomcat uses server.ssl.bundle"]
  S --> M["Decrypted HTTP request reaches Spring MVC"]
  D -- "trusted proxy" --> P["Load balancer or ingress owns public certificate"]
  P --> H["Protected proxy-to-application connection"]
  H --> F["Application handles trusted forwarded information"]
```

sections.title: Use a mounted PKCS12 file through an SSL bundle
sections.content:
```properties
# application.properties
spring.ssl.bundle.jks.web.key.alias=server
spring.ssl.bundle.jks.web.keystore.location=file:/run/secrets/server.p12
spring.ssl.bundle.jks.web.keystore.password=${TLS_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD}
spring.ssl.bundle.jks.web.keystore.type=PKCS12

server.port=8443
server.ssl.bundle=web
```

The password comes from the environment and the keystore is mounted as a protected file. Do not also repeat the same material with direct `server.ssl.key-store*` properties. After startup, test `https://your-host:8443` using the real hostname on the certificate rather than treating `localhost` success as proof of production trust.

questions.question: How does the embedded server lifecycle relate to the Spring ApplicationContext?
questions.title: Embedded server and ApplicationContext lifecycle
questions.direct_answer: A Spring Boot web `ApplicationContext` creates, starts, and stops its embedded server. `ServletWebServerInitializedEvent` reports that the server is ready, but full application readiness comes later at `ApplicationReadyEvent`, after runners finish. Closing the context stops the server; in Boot 3.3.1 graceful shutdown must be enabled with `server.shutdown=graceful` and given a time limit.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The web `ApplicationContext` creates and manages the embedded server.
A `ServletWebServerFactory` supplies the Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow server.
`ServletWebServerInitializedEvent` is useful for the actual listening port.
Server initialized is earlier than `ApplicationReadyEvent`; it is not whole-application readiness.
Closing the context stops the server.
Boot 3.3.1 defaults to immediate shutdown; graceful shutdown is an explicit setting.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
In an embedded Spring Boot application, the web `ApplicationContext` owns the web server. During context refresh, Boot obtains a `ServletWebServerFactory`, creates the server, registers the web application with it, and starts it. The server is not a separate process beside Spring.

After the server is ready, Boot publishes a `ServletWebServerInitializedEvent`. That event is useful for reading the actual port, especially when `server.port=0` asks the operating system for a free port. It does not mean every startup task has finished. `ApplicationReadyEvent` comes later, after application and command-line runners have completed.

Because startup belongs to the context lifecycle, a failure while the context is being created prevents the application from becoming ready. This is safer than treating the HTTP server and Spring beans as unrelated components with separate startup commands.

Closing the `ApplicationContext` also stops the server. In Spring Boot 3.3.1, `server.shutdown` defaults to `immediate`. Setting it to `graceful` makes shutdown part of the earliest phase of stopping `SmartLifecycle` beans: existing requests get a chance to finish while new requests are no longer accepted in the server-specific way.

Graceful shutdown is bounded by `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase`; it is not an unlimited wait. The process also needs to receive a normal termination signal and the load balancer should stop routing new traffic. I use the server event for server facts such as its port and the ready event or readiness state for traffic decisions.

sections.title: Web server events and application readiness
sections.content:
**One owner for beans and the server**

Spring Boot uses a web-specific `ApplicationContext` when it detects a servlet or reactive web application. For the servlet stack, a `ServletWebServerApplicationContext` looks for one `ServletWebServerFactory`. Auto-configuration normally provides a factory for the server found on the classpath.

During context refresh, the factory creates the web server and the context connects the application's servlet components and Spring MVC infrastructure to it. The server is started as part of that refresh process. If startup cannot complete, the application never reaches its ready state.

**Two events answer different questions**

`ServletWebServerInitializedEvent` is published after the servlet web server is ready. It can report the real port, which matters when tests use `server.port=0`. At this point the server exists, but application runners have not necessarily finished.

`ApplicationReadyEvent` is sent later, after `ApplicationRunner` and `CommandLineRunner` work has completed. Boot's readiness state changes to accepting traffic after this stage. A listener that announces the chosen port can use the server event; a platform deciding whether to route requests should use application readiness rather than treating the earlier event as proof.

**Closing the context closes the server**

When the context closes, Boot stops the server as part of the same lifecycle. Boot 3.3.1 uses immediate server shutdown by default. With `server.shutdown=graceful`, the server stops accepting new requests according to its implementation and lets in-flight work complete during a bounded lifecycle phase.

`spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase` supplies that bound. The surrounding platform must still give the process enough termination time and remove it from service discovery or load balancing. A forced process kill cannot complete graceful application cleanup.

sections.title: Startup, readiness, and shutdown are different moments
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  A["SpringApplication.run"] --> C["Web ApplicationContext refresh begins"]
  C --> F["ServletWebServerFactory creates server"]
  F --> S["Server starts"]
  S --> W["ServletWebServerInitializedEvent"]
  W --> T["Application and command-line runners"]
  T --> R["ApplicationReadyEvent and accepting traffic"]
  R --> X["ApplicationContext closes"]
  X --> G{"server.shutdown"}
  G -- "immediate" --> I["Server stops immediately"]
  G -- "graceful" --> B["Bounded drain of in-flight requests"]
```

questions.question: Can you deploy a Spring Boot application as a WAR to an external Tomcat?
questions.title: Spring Boot WAR deployment to external server
questions.direct_answer: Yes, a servlet-based Spring Boot 3.3.1 application can be deployed as a WAR to a compatible external Tomcat. Extend `SpringBootServletInitializer`, set Maven packaging to `war`, and mark the Tomcat starter as `provided`. The external container then owns its port, TLS, and deployment context. Boot 3 requires Java 17 and a Servlet 5.0+ compatible container.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Traditional WAR deployment is supported for servlet-based Spring Boot applications.
Extend `SpringBootServletInitializer` and override `configure`.
Use `<packaging>war</packaging>` and mark the embedded Tomcat starter as `provided`.
The Boot plugin puts provided server libraries in `WEB-INF/lib-provided` for an executable WAR.
External Tomcat owns connector settings and the deployment context.
Boot 3.3.1 requires Java 17 and an external Servlet 5.0+ compatible container.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Yes. A servlet-based Spring Boot 3.3.1 application can be packaged as a WAR and deployed to a compatible external servlet container such as Tomcat. The application class extends `SpringBootServletInitializer`, the build uses `war` packaging, and the Tomcat dependency is marked `provided`.

The external container starts the application through the servlet initializer and its `configure` method. The normal `main` method can remain. With the Spring Boot build plugin, the resulting WAR can also be executable, so the same artifact may be launched with `java -jar` for an embedded run.

`provided` does not simply make Tomcat vanish from a Boot executable WAR. The Boot plugin places provided libraries in `WEB-INF/lib-provided`. An external container does not load them as normal application libraries, which avoids a clash, while Boot's launcher can still use them for `java -jar`.

When the WAR runs in external Tomcat, Tomcat owns connector settings such as ports and TLS and normally controls the deployment context. `server.port` does not reconfigure that shared Tomcat connector. Spring beans, controllers, security, and most application properties remain part of the application.

For the Boot 3.3 line, the baseline is Java 17 and external deployment requires a Servlet 5.0 or later compatible container. Tomcat 9 uses the old `javax.servlet` namespace and is not compatible with a Boot 3 Jakarta application. Traditional WAR deployment is for servlet applications, not a WebFlux-only application. I choose WAR deployment for a real platform requirement, not because external Tomcat is automatically faster.

beats.spokenText: Yes. A servlet-based Spring Boot 3.3.1 application can be packaged as a WAR and deployed to a compatible external servlet container such as Tomcat. The application class extends `SpringBootServletInitializer`, the build uses `war` packaging, and the Tomcat dependency is marked `provided`.

Spring beans, controllers, security, and most application properties remain part of the application.

For the Boot 3.3 line, the baseline is Java 17 and external deployment requires a Servlet 5.0 or later compatible container. Tomcat 9 uses the old `javax.servlet` namespace and is not compatible with a Boot 3 Jakarta application. Traditional WAR deployment is for servlet applications, not a WebFlux-only application. I choose WAR deployment for a real platform requirement, not because external Tomcat is automatically faster.
beats.recallRule: WAR changes who launches and owns the server; it does not replace the Spring application.

sections.title: Prepare one Boot application for two valid launch paths
sections.content:
**Why the application needs another entry point**

An executable Spring Boot application normally begins at `main`. An external servlet container does not call that method to deploy a WAR. It follows the Servlet container startup contract instead. `SpringBootServletInitializer` connects that contract to `SpringApplicationBuilder`, and `configure` names the Boot application source.

Keeping `main` is useful. The external Tomcat path uses the initializer, while an executable WAR can still use the main class when started with `java -jar`.

**How the WAR avoids a server conflict**

The project changes its packaging from JAR to WAR and gives the Tomcat starter `provided` scope. In a normal servlet container, Tomcat already supplies the Servlet engine, so application copies of those server classes must not compete with the container's classes.

The Spring Boot build plugin handles this more carefully than simply deleting the dependency. It puts provided libraries in `WEB-INF/lib-provided`. A standards-based external deployment does not treat that directory as the application's normal `WEB-INF/lib`, but Boot's executable-WAR launcher can still use those libraries for an embedded launch.

**Ownership changes at the deployment boundary**

In embedded mode, application configuration controls the main connector. In external mode, the Tomcat installation owns connector ports, TLS, thread settings, host configuration, and usually the context under which the WAR is deployed. Changing `server.port` inside the WAR does not change the external server's listening port.

The application still owns its Spring beans, controller mappings, security rules, data configuration, and business logic. Teams should document which settings belong to the WAR and which belong to the shared container so that the same property is not expected to control both.

**Check compatibility before deployment**

Spring Boot 3.3.1 has a Java 17 baseline and uses Jakarta Servlet APIs. Its documented traditional-deployment boundary is a Servlet 5.0 or later compatible container. Tomcat 9 is based on the older `javax.servlet` namespace and cannot host the application unchanged. A WebFlux-only application also cannot use traditional servlet WAR deployment.

Choose an external WAR when an existing platform, shared-container policy, or vendor environment requires it. Embedded and external Tomcat use different ownership models; neither is automatically faster. Measure the actual deployment and include container configuration in the test plan.

sections.title: What changes between embedded and external Tomcat?
sections.content:
| Concern | Executable application | WAR in external Tomcat |
|---|---|---|
| Startup | `main` calls `SpringApplication.run` | Container calls `SpringBootServletInitializer` |
| Server libraries | Used from the executable archive | Container provides its server classes |
| Port and TLS | Application `server.*` configuration | External Tomcat connector configuration |
| Context path | Application/server configuration | Chosen by external deployment configuration |
| Artifact | Executable JAR or WAR | Deployable WAR |

sections.title: Minimal Maven and application changes for WAR deployment
sections.content:
```xml
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>3.3.1</version>
        <relativePath/>
    </parent>

    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>orders</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>
    <packaging>war</packaging>

    <properties>
        <java.version>17</java.version>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
            <scope>provided</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
```

```java
package com.example.orders;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.builder.SpringApplicationBuilder;
import org.springframework.boot.web.servlet.support.SpringBootServletInitializer;

@SpringBootApplication
public class OrderApplication extends SpringBootServletInitializer {
    @Override
    protected SpringApplicationBuilder configure(SpringApplicationBuilder application) {
        return application.sources(OrderApplication.class);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(OrderApplication.class, args);
    }
}
```

`mvn package` produces the WAR. Test both the target external Tomcat and, if the executable path is supported by the deployment plan, `java -jar target/orders-1.0.0.war`.
